papers.title: Predicting transcriptional interactions with GrnPFN
papers.abstract: Combinatorial therapies offer opportunities to improve treatment efficacy and overcome therapeutic resistance, but their rational design requires understanding how combined interventions interact beyond their individual effects. Combined genetic and chemical perturbations can elicit nonadditive transcriptional responses, yet the vast number of possible combinations limits experimental characterization. Predicting these interactions is particularly challenging when few or no combinations have been measured. Here we present GrnPFN, a prior-data fitted network that predicts nonadditive transcriptional responses to combinations from single-perturbation profiles. Pretrained on simulated screens generated from random gene-regulatory networks, GrnPFN incorporates measured combinations through in-context learning without retraining. We evaluated GrnPFN in single-cell screens spanning CRISPR activation, RNA knockdown and drug combinations, using separate cells to construct model inputs, training targets and test targets. Without measured combinations in the target screen, GrnPFN outperformed gradient boosting trained on other screens. With limited combination measurements, it outperformed kernel ridge regression fitted to the same measured pairs. These advantages extended to an additional screen combining CRISPR interference with a drug. Our results demonstrate that pretraining on simulated regulatory networks enables prediction of nonadditive transcriptional interactions across perturbation modalities when experimental measurements are scarce.

papers.title: PathwayDesigner: an interactive SBML/KEGG/Reactome/Escher compatible editor for biochemical network diagrams
papers.abstract: PathwayDesigner is an interactive editor for biochemical network diagrams. A network can be drawn directly on the screen, or described as an Antimony model, which PathwayDesigner then lays out and draws. PathwayDesigner reads and writes SBML using the Layout and Render packages, writing Render in a form that other tools can interpret correctly. PathwayDesigner can read and write a diagram's layout and appearance using either Antimony's own layout statements or in a new, more concise format that we propose. PathwayDesigner can also open Escher maps, KEGG maps and Reactome's SBML-based maps. Other components of the model, such as events, rules, functions, and units, are kept and can be edited within the application. Species and reactions can be annotated with references to any database, and PathwayDesigner can find and add annotation references automatically by searching the BiGG, ChEBI, PubChem, and Rhea databases with a component's Id or Display Name, or contextually with a reaction's reactants and products. The network's stoichiometry matrix, conservation laws, and flux null space are computed and visualized on the diagram. The visual style of a diagram can be set with named styles or themes, saved and reused across models. One built-in theme follows the Escher style. The software is written in pure Rust as one code base for Windows, macOS, Linux, and the web browser, where it runs as WebAssembly. The web version is hosted on a GitHub page so that a user doesn't need to manually install code. All 1,062 curated BioModels models and the 1,823 semantic cases of the SBML Test Suite were read and written back without change. Diagrams were exchanged in both directions with COPASI and SBMLNetwork. PathwayDesigner is released as open source with MIT licence, at https://github.com/sys-bio/PathwayDesigner-rs, and runs in the browser at https://sys-bio.github.io/PathwayDesigner-rs/.

papers.title: The impact of DNA replication on the timing of cellular events
papers.abstract: Cellular timing often relies on the accumulation of a regulatory protein to a threshold. For a stable protein produced at a constant rate, the threshold alone sets timing precision: the squared coefficient of variation of the first-passage time is the inverse of the threshold number of molecules. This counting limit appears to be a fundamental constraint. However, production rates vary across the cell cycle. By solving exactly a stochastic model coupling DNA replication and protein accumulation, we show that when a gene replicates at an optimal time, precision exceeds the counting limit.

papers.title: A disease-contextualized atlas of proteome-scale molecular influences of natural products
papers.abstract: Understanding the system-wide molecular effects of natural products remains challenging because chemical knowledge is fragmented, proteomic coverage is incomplete, and experimental perturbation data are scarce, particularly for multicomponent medicinal herbs. Here we present an integrative framework for modeling molecular influences of natural compounds and medicinal herbs in disease-specific contexts. We harmonized three herbal medicine databases to establish a standardized atlas of 46,422 chemical entities, 12,459 medicinal herbs, and 156,588 herb-compound associations. We integrated high-confidence protein-protein interactions with proteomic and transcriptomic data to reconstruct molecular networks across nine cancers. By prioritizing protein-level evidence and using transcriptomic associations to extend coverage, these networks capture disease-associated interaction rewiring beyond differential expression. We coupled AI-inferred compound-target interactions with signed random walks with restart to model the propagation of molecular influences from sparse direct targets to directional, genome-scale network profiles. Using gastric cancer as an in-depth case study, we generated profiles for 45,418 compounds across 16,899 molecular nodes and explored multicomponent herbal interventions. We further applied the framework to eight additional cancers and retrospectively compared selected profiles with published drug-perturbation proteomics. This atlas provides a scalable basis for systems-level modeling of natural-product interventions and mechanism-guided drug discovery.

papers.title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
papers.abstract: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.
